highlights: State control over hydrocarbons remains strong

frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: European demand for Algerian gas provides revenue and diplomatic leverage, but exposes Algiers to pricing pressure and external expectations over supply reliability.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY BELT
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: CHINA DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE LEGACY
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain embedded in Angola's infrastructure, constraining policy flexibility despite efforts to diversify lenders and renegotiate exposure.

frictionVectors.title: LOBITO CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the corridor increases Angola's strategic value as a route for Congolese and Zambian minerals, while creating pressure over governance, access, and security.

highlights: Cotonou remains a pivotal trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: NIGER BORDER AND TRADE DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Niger and volatile cross-border commerce threaten port throughput and regional supply chains, increasing Benin's reliance on alternative diplomatic channels.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL MILITANT SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups operating near Burkina Faso and Niger are expanding pressure on northern communities and transport corridors, drawing increased foreign security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: DIAMOND MARKET DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence through its state partnership with De Beers, but weak global diamond demand exposes national revenues to external market cycles.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS AND WATER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: New mining and energy projects could broaden the resource base, yet scarce water and power infrastructure increase dependence on foreign capital and technical partners.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD NATIONALIZATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The junta is tightening state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold, but weak administrative capacity and informal networks continue to divert production and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Expanded cooperation with Russian-linked security actors reduces reliance on Western partners but creates new political, financial, and operational dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Security Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border activity continue to constrain regional trade and security cooperation. The dispute increases Burundi's dependence on selected external diplomatic and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but limited capital and regulatory capacity leave room for opaque foreign-linked concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Port and Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde benefits from strategic Atlantic infrastructure and partnerships, but its ports, maritime surveillance, and connectivity remain reliant on external financing and operators.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on tourism, imported fuel, and climate-sensitive infrastructure limits effective sovereign control over key economic resources. External shocks can quickly affect fiscal and energy security.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon, timber, and mining sectors remain vulnerable to opaque contracting and foreign commercial influence, reducing the state's ability to capture full strategic value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts infrastructure, agricultural production, and transport corridors. Instability also complicates external investment around the Kribi port and regional trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-for-Resources Model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel remain central to regime protection and counterinsurgency, while mining and commercial arrangements raise concerns over opaque access to gold and diamonds.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country depends heavily on neighboring states and foreign-backed routes for fuel, food, and exports. Conflict spillovers from Sudan and instability along western corridors constrain sovereign economic planning.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Sector and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances remain heavily exposed to oil production and export infrastructure controlled through foreign-linked commercial arrangements. Price volatility and contract asymmetries limit autonomous resource management.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Chad is recalibrating longstanding French security ties while managing relations with Russia, the United States, and regional partners. Instability in Sudan and the Sahel places additional pressure on border security and state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: French Presence and Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a major sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' control over surrounding maritime assets. Migration pressures further complicate bilateral relations.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros remains dependent on external financing, remittances, and imported energy, leaving infrastructure and resource policy vulnerable to foreign leverage.

highlights: Eastern security crisis undermines state control

frictionVectors.title: Mining Control and Foreign Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, coltan, and gold production continues to attract intense competition among multinational firms, neighboring states, and foreign-backed supply chains. Weak enforcement allows significant value leakage and informal extraction.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to limit Kinshasa's control over territory, transport corridors, and mineral zones. Regional military involvement and competing diplomatic initiatives complicate sovereign security decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on oil exports, exposing national policy to price cycles, production-sharing arrangements, and foreign energy operators. Limited diversification constrains autonomous resource strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resources Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and lending provide essential connectivity but increase long-term financial and strategic dependence. Debt servicing and project transparency remain sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large external investors remain important in hydrocarbons, mining, telecommunications, and infrastructure. Abidjan is improving regulatory capacity, but strategic sectors remain exposed to foreign ownership and financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability along the Burkina Faso and Mali borders threaten transport corridors, agricultural zones, and investor confidence. Security spending and external partnerships are expanding in response.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's concentration of American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates revenue and diplomatic leverage but constrains independent security maneuver. Rivalry among outside powers raises escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and logistics remain central to the economy and are closely linked to foreign capital, especially Chinese financing and regional trade flows. Debt exposure and competition with neighboring corridors limit sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Gulf financing
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and currency shortages increase reliance on IMF programs and Gulf investment, giving external partners influence over strategic assets and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute with Ethiopia over GERD operations keeps Egypt exposed to upstream water-management decisions and regional power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Declining or volatile hydrocarbon output leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, external markets, and opaque revenue arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and financing provide essential infrastructure but deepen creditor and contractor dependence without creating broad domestic productive capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector externalization
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects depend on foreign technical and investment partners, creating tension between sovereign control, revenue capture, and international scrutiny.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Gulf, Western, and regional actors for Red Sea access increases pressure on Eritrea to trade port access and diplomatic alignment for security and investment.

frictionVectors.title: South African corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, fuel supply, finance, and transport links remain heavily tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room for autonomous economic strategy.

frictionVectors.title: SACU revenue vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Southern African Customs Union transfers exposes the government to regional downturns and constrains fiscal sovereignty when external revenue falls.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects remain linked to Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral financing, creating refinancing exposure and external leverage over development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and regional security competition
frictionVectors.details: GERD operations, Sudan instability, and tensions with Egypt and Somalia place Ethiopia's water, trade, and security infrastructure at the center of sustained regional contestation.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-Mineral Concession Control
frictionVectors.details: The civilianized post-coup government is seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese and oil while balancing established French, Chinese, and multinational interests. Limited processing capacity constrains immediate bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon’s mining exports remain dependent on externally financed rail and port infrastructure. Maintenance and expansion decisions could give foreign operators substantial influence over export flows and state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and weak monitoring risk reducing local access to coastal resources. Chinese-linked fleets and opaque licensing remain politically sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Border and Trade Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia’s transport, food, and energy links remain closely tied to Senegal. Border disruptions or asymmetrical infrastructure negotiations can quickly constrain Banjul’s policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Environmental Loss
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining continues to damage water systems and undermine formal state control over land and mineral revenues. Foreign-backed supply chains and local political protection complicate enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and External Financing Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF conditions limit Accra’s flexibility over energy, mining, and infrastructure policy. The government is trying to increase local processing and public value capture without losing access to external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is concentrating foreign capital, rail, and port influence in a single export corridor involving major international partners. Guinea’s state participation may rise, but dependence on external operators remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Value-Capture Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conakry is pressing mining companies for infrastructure, local processing, and higher fiscal returns while relying heavily on foreign firms and logistics networks. Political uncertainty increases the risk of abrupt contract reviews and investor retaliation.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Most value from Guinea-Bissau’s cashew sector is captured outside the country through foreign buyers, traders, and processing networks. Limited storage, finance, and domestic processing leave producers exposed to external price and logistics shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Weak naval and regulatory capacity enables contested fishing access and suspected illicit maritime activity. Foreign fleets and opaque licensing arrangements continue to challenge Bissau’s control over coastal resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Fiscal Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and IMF-linked reforms constrain Nairobi's policy space. Chinese infrastructure lending remains strategically important, even as Kenya seeks more diversified financing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Northern Corridor face competition from Tanzanian routes and Gulf-linked investment. Control of logistics infrastructure remains central to Kenya's regional sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but bind Lesotho's fiscal position and infrastructure planning to Pretoria. Dam construction and project financing remain vulnerable to delays and cost pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho relies heavily on South African markets, remittances, electricity links, and customs arrangements. This limits independent bargaining power despite formal sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining, particularly in Nimba and western Liberia, offers export revenue but leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, concession terms, and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and associated logistics networks attract foreign commercial influence. Weak domestic infrastructure and limited fiscal capacity reduce Liberia's leverage in negotiations.

frictionVectors.title: Divided Control of Oil Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed groups can disrupt production, export terminals, and revenue flows. Libya's oil wealth finances rival power centers more than a unified sovereign state.

frictionVectors.title: External Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf actors, and European states retain influence through security partnerships, contractors, migration policy, and energy interests. Their involvement constrains national control over strategic decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and mineral-sands projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented concessions. The government faces pressure to increase local value addition and fiscal returns without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak roads constrain domestic processing and leave mining projects reliant on dedicated infrastructure. External lenders and operators therefore retain substantial influence over strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: MINING-SECTOR FOREIGN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking greater state participation and local processing in uranium, graphite, and rare-earth projects, but financing, technology, and export access remain heavily dependent on foreign firms and donors.

frictionVectors.title: IMPORT-DEPENDENT ENERGY SYSTEM
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported fuel and vulnerable electricity infrastructure constrains economic sovereignty, while foreign-exchange shortages complicate access to essential energy and industrial inputs.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD-CONCESSION CONFRONTATION
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is renegotiating mining terms and asserting a larger state share, creating sustained friction with international operators while gold remains vital to public finances.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support increases external leverage over strategic decisions, while insurgent violence threatens roads, mining zones, and trade routes.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE GAS PARTNERSHIP DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers new revenue and diplomatic leverage, but Mauritania remains dependent on foreign capital, operators, and export infrastructure to monetize its gas resources.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND FISHERIES ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in iron ore and fishing generates revenue but limits domestic value capture, while disputes over access and distribution remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS IMPLEMENTATION RISKS
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago strengthens its diplomatic position, but the future of the Diego Garcia base and the terms of any UK-US arrangement remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: IMPORTED ENERGY EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: The island remains dependent on imported fuel and vulnerable to maritime disruptions, limiting full control over its energy security despite strong institutions and diversified trade.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and investment in Western Sahara underpin its phosphate, fisheries, and infrastructure strategy, but contested sovereignty creates legal and diplomatic exposure with external partners.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN CAPITAL AND WATER STRESS
frictionVectors.details: Large renewable-energy, automotive, port, and logistics projects deepen Morocco's industrial capacity while also creating dependence on foreign investors and intensifying competition over scarce water.

highlights: LNG ambitions constrained by Cabo Delgado insecurity
Resource bargaining with external energy partners

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security and LNG Access
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten gas infrastructure, transport corridors, and local legitimacy. External security support remains central, limiting Maputo's independent control over project timelines and operating conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed coal, graphite, logistics, and energy projects provide investment but reinforce dependence on external capital and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium, and other mineral projects are attracting major foreign investors. Windhoek is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns while avoiding policy shifts that could deter capital.

frictionVectors.title: Green-Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European and other external partners are shaping port, power, and hydrogen development. Namibia must prevent an export enclave model and secure domestic industrial benefits.

highlights: Junta consolidates control over strategic resources
Western exit accelerates Russian and regional alignment

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing foreign mining interests for greater state control and revenue, particularly in uranium. The confrontation risks investment withdrawal, legal disputes, and reduced production.

frictionVectors.title: Security Partnerships and Export Corridors
frictionVectors.details: The departure of Western forces and deeper ties with Russia and the Alliance of Sahel States are reshaping military and infrastructure access. Persistent insurgency continues to disrupt roads, energy links, and mineral logistics.

highlights: Oil-sector reform meets entrenched extraction losses

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Foreign-Operator Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline sabotage, crude theft, and aging infrastructure weaken state capture of petroleum value. International oil companies remain important, while production-sharing and divestment disputes limit Abuja's leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and multilateral financing is expanding roads, rail, ports, and electricity capacity. Debt, concession terms, and local-content enforcement remain central sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Mineral-state ambitions collide with regional scrutiny
Security influence expands across the Great Lakes

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral and Security Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security role and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to trigger regional and Western pressure. Sanctions, diplomatic isolation, or tighter traceability rules could affect Kigali's resource strategy.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Strategic Autonomy
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development model relies on foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships while emphasizing state control. Conditional financing and reputational pressure increasingly constrain policy space.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest has not yet translated into commercial production, leaving São Tomé and Príncipe reliant on aid, tourism, and fisheries. International operators could shape licensing terms before the state develops stronger negotiating capacity.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The country’s maritime zone attracts interest from Portugal, China, and Gulf of Guinea security partners. Limited naval capacity constrains enforcement against illegal fishing and unauthorized activity.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN-LED HYDROCARBON PROJECTS
frictionVectors.details: Sangomar oil and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas are expanding state revenues but remain dependent on foreign operators, technology, and project finance. Dakar is seeking greater domestic participation while managing production delays and revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE GOVERNANCE PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The government faces pressure to renegotiate contracts, increase transparency, and ensure that new hydrocarbons support public services and industrialization. Fiscal demands and political expectations could strain relations with investors.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND EEZ CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access remains central to food security and revenue, but limited surveillance capacity leaves Seychelles vulnerable to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing. The state is trying to capture more value through monitoring, licensing, and sustainable marine finance.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: India, China, France, and other partners compete for maritime access and security relationships around the archipelago. Seychelles must preserve strategic autonomy while relying on external support for coastal surveillance and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINERAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other minerals remain major sources of foreign exchange, leaving fiscal stability exposed to commodity prices and multinational operating decisions. The government is under pressure to improve local processing, taxation, and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors are important to mining, roads, ports, and energy projects. Contract transparency, debt exposure, and land-use disputes remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: TURKEY-BACKED ENERGY AND SECURITY ROLE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey’s expanding defense, maritime, and energy relationship gives Mogadishu useful capacity but also creates long-term dependence on an external patron. Offshore exploration is politically sensitive amid disputes over federal authority and revenue sharing.

frictionVectors.title: FEDERAL RESOURCE CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The central government’s licensing ambitions face resistance from federal member states and unresolved constitutional questions. Weak maritime enforcement and al-Shabaab activity further limit Somalia’s ability to secure infrastructure and capture resource value.

highlights: Grid and port bottlenecks weaken strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial platinum, manganese and chromium assets, but foreign capital and limited domestic processing reduce sovereign control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and logistics crisis
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power, rail constraints and congested ports undermine mining exports and increase dependence on external financing and technology.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to regional conflict

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving its principal revenue stream vulnerable to war, transit bargaining and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector foreign leverage
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies and neighboring states retain major influence over production, payments and transport while domestic institutions struggle to capture stable public revenue.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and transport corridors

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks outside state control
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide financing to armed actors and create openings for foreign traders, intermediaries and patrons to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan, refineries and oil transit infrastructure, giving regional powers leverage over humanitarian access, exports and reconstruction.

highlights: Resource nationalism paired with selective investment
Ports and gas projects expand strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking to convert major offshore gas reserves into domestic industrial value, but negotiations with international investors and financing partners remain central to project control.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Upgraded ports and rail links attract Gulf, Chinese and other foreign interests, creating leverage over export corridors while improving Tanzania's regional bargaining position.

highlights: Lomé consolidates as a regional trade hub
Phosphate wealth under limited domestic value capture

frictionVectors.title: Port dependency and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's importance as a Gulf of Guinea and Sahel gateway brings strategic revenue but also exposes customs, logistics and security infrastructure to external operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector leverage
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a core sovereign asset, yet technology, finance and downstream-processing gaps limit domestic capture of the sector's full value.

highlights: Phosphate and energy sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: European energy and migration leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European trade, financing, and migration cooperation while facing pressure to manage irregular migration routes. Energy import dependence limits room for autonomous policy.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector stagnation
frictionVectors.details: Production disruptions and weak investment have reduced the state’s ability to convert phosphate reserves into reliable public revenue. Labor unrest and aging infrastructure continue to constrain recovery.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert oil corridor
frictionVectors.details: The oil project and planned export pipeline are strengthening Uganda’s fiscal prospects but increasing environmental, land, and sovereignty disputes. Dependence on foreign capital and regional transit infrastructure limits domestic control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: External financing concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects provide critical infrastructure while adding repayment and strategic-dependence risks. Western sanctions and governance pressure further complicate Uganda’s financing options.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking more domestic processing and stronger state participation in copper and cobalt while competing investors from China, the United States, and the Gulf seek supply-chain access. Regulatory credibility and power availability remain decisive.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and rail constraints threaten mineral output and export diversification. Regional corridors and imported electricity remain vulnerable to financing, climate, and political disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum control
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is pushing local beneficiation and tighter mineral rules, especially for lithium, but remains dependent on foreign companies, technology, and markets. Policy unpredictability and sanctions complicate efforts to retain more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Power and currency fragility
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and recurring currency instability raise operating costs across mining and agriculture. Reliance on regional power imports and external hard-currency earnings constrains sovereign economic control.
